### 2.1 CadEval (cadeval)

`data/benchmarks/engineering-design/cadeval.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-18 · last verified 2026-11-18

*LLMs write OpenSCAD for 25 simple mechanical parts; a part passes if its rendered mesh matches a reference within 1 mm.*

A text-to-CAD benchmark built by one person in April 2025 and published as a GitHub repository with a results dashboard. Each of the 25 tasks describes a single, simple mechanical part in prose, usually as numbered modelling steps with every dimension given (a hex nut, a plate with two holes, an eye bolt, a T-handle tap holder, a silo with a hole through it), written so that only one geometry is a correct reading. The maintainer modelled each reference part in Autodesk Fusion 360 and exported it as an STL mesh, and tallied how many manual operations it took, from one to five. A model receives the description with a system prompt in one API call and must return an OpenSCAD script, which OpenSCAD renders to an STL; Zoo's text-to-CAD service, the one non-LLM entrant, returns the STL directly. The rendered mesh is aligned to the reference with ICP and passes only if all six checks hold: watertight, the expected number of connected components, the aligned bounding box within 1 mm, volume within 2%, Chamfer distance at most 1 mm and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance at most 1 mm. The headline is the overall pass rate over every task and replicate, with failed generations and renders counted as failures, reported beside estimated cost and time per attempt. The published run of 2025-04-22 tested 15 systems with two replicates per task: o3 led at 74% (37 of 50), reasoning models took the top six places, Zoo scored 20%, and two tasks (an eye bolt and a square-to-circle loft) were never passed. Epoch AI republishes those 15 rows on its benchmarking hub and fits them in its Capabilities Index. The repository has not been pushed since May 2025; CadQueryEval, a separate CadQuery port of the same 25 tasks, ran 91 models in 2026 and was archived as saturated when four scored 100%.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `code/function-synthesis` · S1
  - why: The model writes an OpenSCAD program, but the program is the means; the checks score the mesh it renders to against the reference, and no test exercises the program. The code family's exclusion ("code is the means to a result in another field") applies.
  > Calculates the Chamfer distance between generated and reference point clouds after ICP alignment
- `domain` not `reasoning-general/spatial-reasoning` · [S3][cadeval-s3]
  - why: The write-up names poor spatial reasoning as one failure mode, but the tasks are CAD parts scored by geometric fidelity, not spatial puzzles posed to study the ability.
  > Task 11 is a good example of poor spatial reasoning.
- `capability` not `constraint-satisfaction` · [S3][cadeval-s3]
  - why: Any one failed check fails the attempt, which meets the inclusion test's letter, but four of the six conditions are tolerances of closeness to one reference shape rather than the prompt's stated requirements, and the sources claim geometric accuracy, which generation-fidelity carries (review\_checks).
  > all of the geometric checks must be passed.
- `capability` not `spatial-reasoning` · [S3][cadeval-s3]
  - why: Turning step-by-step prose into placed solids needs spatial inference, and the write-up blames poor spatial reasoning for one task's failures, but the scored quantity is the fidelity of the result to a reference, which the term's exclusion sends elsewhere (review\_checks).
  > Task 11 is a good example of poor spatial reasoning.
- `capability` not `reliability-consistency` · [S3][cadeval-s3]
  - why: Each task runs twice in the published run, but the replicates are averaged into the pass rate, which the term's exclusion rules out.
  > In the eval run, 15 different models were tested on the 25 tasks with 2 replicates were task.
- `capability` not `tool-use` · [S3][cadeval-s3]
  - why: No tools are offered; the model answers in one API call.
  > For each task and model, the eval sends the text prompt (along with a system prompt) to the LLM via API.
- `evaluation_method` not `model-graded-judge` · S1
  - why: No model takes part in grading; the checks are geometry computations in Open3D.
  > Checks if the mesh is manifold using Open3D.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `reasoning-model` · S1
  - why: The README notes that the thinking budget moves results, but the benchmark is not built around a reasoning setting; the budget is a run condition (comparability), as for mmlu-pro.

### 2.2 Parametric CAD Bench (parametric-cad-bench)

`data/benchmarks/engineering-design/parametric-cad-bench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-18 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Agents author editable FreeCAD parts from text or engineering drawings, scored on geometry and named dimensions.*

A benchmark from gNucleus AI in which AI agents author parametric CAD parts in FreeCAD. The agent works in a sandboxed container with FreeCAD and a shell: it writes a Python script that builds the part as a feature tree (sketches, pads, pockets, patterns) in a single PartDesign body and saves a native .FCStd document, running and revising it as it likes until it stops or the time limit (9,000 seconds in V3) ends the trial. A separate verifier, the open-source gnucleus-freecad-validator, scores the saved document on two axes: geometry similarity to a held-back reference model (volume, surface areas, surface types, moments of inertia and aligned face centres, behind bounding-box and structural gates) and consistency with the part's specification (each key parameter must be measurable in the document as a named dimension, within 1% by default, with a budget of ten failures). The two are combined by harmonic mean, so a part that looks right but exposes no named dimensions scores zero, and the headline is the mean reward over all tasks with failures counted as zero. Entrants are complete agent-model systems (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Antigravity, mini-swe-agent and, in V1, Gemini CLI), and the harness is treated as a variable under test. V1 (May 2026) had 100 text-to-CAD creation tasks on FreeCAD 0.21.2. V2 (September 2026) re-ran the same 100 tasks on FreeCAD 1.1.0, with the held-out assets moved into a separate verifier image and the validator updated. V3 (September 2026, current) is a new set of 100 tasks: 30 text-to-CAD creation, 30 create-and-edit (build a part from text, then modify it; both models are scored) and 40 reconstructions of parts from engineering drawings, with a stricter scorer and no agent network beyond the model provider. Each version keeps its own board, and only V3 takes submissions. On the V3 snapshot of 2026-09-24, Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 leads at 61.03%.

- `capability` = self-correction · [S3][parametric-cad-bench-s3]

### 2.3 AnalogGym (analoggym)

`data/benchmarks/engineering-design/analoggym.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-18 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Analog circuit sizing on 30 topologies, each design simulated in SPICE across PVT corners and scored against baselines.*

A testing suite for machine-learning methods of analog integrated-circuit sizing, from a team at Fudan University, the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China and three other Chinese institutions, presented as an invited paper at ICCAD 2024. It holds 30 circuit topologies in five categories: amplifiers, low-dropout regulators (LDOs), sensing front ends, voltage references and phase-locked loops (the paper's table lists 16, 6, 6, 3 and 1, which is 32). Each circuit ships as an encapsulated SPICE netlist with its complete bias circuitry, a testbench and a file of design variables: transistor widths, lengths and multipliers, capacitors, resistors and bias currents. A sizing method proposes values, the testbench simulates the circuit (DC, AC, pole-zero and transient analyses) at chosen process, voltage and temperature (PVT) corners, and scripts extract the metrics, such as gain, phase margin, PSRR, CMRR, noise, offset, settling time, power and area. The amplifiers and LDOs run on the open-source Ngspice simulator with the SkyWater sky130 PDK; the other three categories need Cadence Spectre or Synopsys HSPICE and process models that are not open. For amplifiers the paper defines a reference figure of merit, FOM\_AMP, which multiplies each metric's ratio to the baseline of the topology's original paper (Table 6) and penalises noise, temperature coefficient and offset worse than baseline; a design should beat the baseline on every metric, with the phase margin between 45 and 90 degrees. In May 2025 the maintainers rewrote the penalty, because the printed indicator-function form zeroes the product. The paper's own study sizes four three-stage amplifiers in sky130 with five methods (graph-network RL, two Bayesian optimisers, two evolutionary algorithms), ten runs each under a stated limit of 1,000 simulations, the evolutionary methods at four worst-case PVT corners; constrained Voronoi tree search reaches the highest single-objective FOM\_AMP on all four. There is no leaderboard; others report results in their own papers, such as an AAAI-26 RL method scored by FOM\_AMP on seven of the circuits over 20 PVT corners.

### 2.4 CircuitNet (circuitnet)

`data/benchmarks/engineering-design/circuitnet.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-10 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Chip layouts from real RISC-V designs, for predicting routing congestion, DRC violations and IR drop early in the flow.*

A dataset for machine learning in VLSI physical design. Open RISC-V designs were taken through logic synthesis and place-and-route with commercial EDA tools under thousands of settings (CircuitNet 1.0 has 10,242 layouts at 28 nm). Features are extracted at each design stage, as image-like maps and graph netlists. The tasks predict, from early-stage features, what later stages will show: routing congestion, design-rule-check violations, IR drop and, from 2.0, net delay and timing. Each task is scored with the metric of the method it reproduces: NRMSE and SSIM for congestion, ROC and precision-recall AUC for DRC violations and IR-drop hotspots, R² for net delay. CircuitNet 2.0 (ICLR 2024) moves to a 14 nm FinFET node with CPU, GPU and AI-chip designs, more than 10,000 samples in all. CircuitNet 3.0 (ICLR 2026), whose corresponding authors are at the Chinese Academy of Sciences' State Key Lab of Processors and CUHK, with Peking University co-authors, collects 8,659 open-source RTL designs, augments them to 15,863 instances at 45 nm, and predicts post-layout timing (arrival time, WNS, TNS) from RTL and power from RTL and netlists, scored by Pearson correlation, R² and MAPE on a fixed design-level split.

  > CircuitNet, which provides holistic support for cross-stage prediction tasks in back-end design with diverse samples
- `released` = 2022-08-01 · [S2][circuitnet-s2]
  > \- 2022/8/1 First release.

#### circuitnet · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary engineering-design/circuit-eda · [S1][circuitnet-s1]
  - why: Every task predicts a property of a chip layout in the physical-design flow, which is electronic design automation.
  > we further conducted experiments on three prediction tasks: congestion, design rule check (DRC) violation, and IR drop
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S1][circuitnet-s1]
  - why: A model predicts a physical layout's later state -- routing congestion, rule violations, voltage drop -- from early-stage features, scored against what the EDA tools computed. The term's definition names physical, chemical, biological and Earth systems; a chip layout is taken as a physical system here, which a reviewer may contest.
  > cross-stage prediction was introduced to replace the original long feedback loops between design stages with local loops within the design stages
- `evaluation_method` = statistical-fit, classification-metric · [S1][circuitnet-s1]
  - why: Congestion is scored by NRMSE and SSIM over the predicted map; DRC violations and IR-drop hotspots by ROC and precision-recall AUC.
  > we considered the area under the curve (AUC) of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and that of the precision-recall (PR) curve as the metrics for imbalanced learning
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model · [S1][circuitnet-s1]
  - why: The entrants are models trained from scratch for EDA prediction tasks, and engineering-design is one of the disciplines domain-specialist-model names.
  > These methods utilized image-like features to train a generative model, such as fully convolutional networks (FCNs) and U-Net

#### circuitnet · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system FCN-based congestion predictor (reimplemented) · [S1][circuitnet-s1]
  > The corresponding results for an FCN based method \[3\] were 0.040 and 0.80, respectively
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · [S2][circuitnet-s2]
  - why: The features, labels and code are public; producing new layouts would need commercial EDA licences, but scoring on the released data does not.
  > This repository is intended to hosts codes and demos for CircuitNet
- `task` = exists true; input image-like feature maps (and netlist graphs) extracted from a layout at an early design stage, RTL code, and for power the synthesised netlist as well (3.0); output A predicted map or set of hotspots for a later stage -- congestion, DRC violations, IR drop -- net delays (2.0), or post-layout timing metrics and power (3.0).; scoring Per task, the original method's metrics (NRMSE and SSIM; ROC and PR AUC); R² for net delay (2.0); Pearson correlation, R² and MAPE for timing and power (3.0). · [S1][circuitnet-s1]
  > we used the normalized root-mean-square-error and structural similarity index measure as metrics to evaluate pixel-level accuracy
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = fully-automatable · [S2][circuitnet-s2]
  - why: Training and scoring on the released data runs end to end with the repository's scripts.
  > python test.py --task congestion\_gpdl --pretrained PRETRAINED\_WEIGHTS\_PATH
- `execution.harness` = CircuitNet (test.py per task) · [S2][circuitnet-s2]
  > python test.py --task congestion\_gpdl --pretrained PRETRAINED\_WEIGHTS\_PATH

#### circuitnet · Data and licence

- `data.access` = fully-open · [S2][circuitnet-s2]
  - why: Every version is a public download (Google Drive, Baidu Netdisk, Hugging Face), apart from 3.0's layout artifacts still being uploaded (access\_note).
  > CircuitNet-N14 (v2.0) is currently maintained on Hugging Face
- `data.refresh` = versioned-releases · [S3][circuitnet-s3]
  - why: New technology nodes and fixes arrive in dated, numbered releases recorded in the changelog.
  > CircuitNet 1.0 Paper Link RTL to Layout in 28 nm Planar CMOS. CircuitNet 2.0 Paper Link RTL to Layout in 14 nm FinFET. CircuitNet 3.0
- `data.data_provenance` = simulation-generated, web-scraped · [S1][circuitnet-s1]
  > Then, the physical design transformed the netlists into layouts with Cadence Innovus
- `data.contamination_evidence` = stance against · [S4][circuitnet-s4]
  > Source-level train/validation/test partitioning, with augmented variants of test sources excluded from train/val to avoid leakage
- `execution.code_licence` = BSD-3-Clause · [S2][circuitnet-s2]
  > This repository is released under the BSD 3-Clause. license as found in the LICENSE file

#### circuitnet · Governance and independence

- `governance.maintainer` = The CircuitNet team (School of Integrated Circuits, Peking University) · [S3][circuitnet-s3]
  - why: The authors are at Peking University's School of Integrated Circuits, and the site and code are the CircuitNet team's.
  > Copyright © 2022-present CircuitNet Team

#### circuitnet · Lifecycle and activity

- `lifecycle` = active · [S2][circuitnet-s2]
  - why: The maintainers released CircuitNet 3.0 in May 2026 and keep the code updated.
  > Released CircuitNet 3.0 with N45 PDK!
- `activity` = no-submission-channel · [S3][circuitnet-s3]
  - why: The site and the README offer the data, documentation, tutorials and code, and no leaderboard or results route; results appear in users' papers.
  > Home DocsDocs Get Started Dataset Features Tutorial Download GitHub

**Open review checks** (5):

1. capability scientific-prediction for an engineered system (see its basis).
2. (field `data.dataset_licence`) dataset\_licence is null although each Hugging Face release declares one (3.0 apache-2.0, N14 bsd-3-clause) and 1.0 states none. Once versions are recorded, the licence can go per version; or the field could take 3.0's, the release dataset\_url points to, with the others in the note. · S5
   > license: bsd-3-clause
3. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk stays unknown for the family. 3.0 ships a source-level split that keeps augmented copies of test designs out of training, which argues for low on 3.0 alone, while 1.0 and 2.0 leave the split to the user's configuration. · [S4][circuitnet-s4]
   > Source-level train/validation/test partitioning, with augmented variants of test sources excluded from train/val to avoid leakage
4. (field `lineage`) Lineage: 3.0 may be a separate benchmark rather than a version. Its paper's corresponding authors are at the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Computing Technology and at CUHK (the title block, kept out of the extract), its data and code sit in the SKLP-EDA-LAB organisations rather than circuitnet, and its tasks (timing and power from RTL, scored by PCC, R² and MAPE) differ from 1.0's and 2.0's layout tasks; 04 S4 sends a different maintainer to a new entry with a lineage link. Against that, the CircuitNet README and site list it as the family's 3.0, and Peking University authors share the paper. · [S6][circuitnet-s6]
   > 1State Key Lab of Processors, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences 2University of Chinese Academy of Sciences 3The Chinese University of Hong Kong 4Peking University 5Stanford University ∗Equal contribution †Corresponding authors
5. (field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance web-scraped is 3.0's alone (RTL harvested from public repositories). Its augmented instances come from rule-based syntax-tree rewriting, which synthetic-procedural may also describe; if 3.0 leaves this entry, web-scraped goes with it. · [S6][circuitnet-s6]
   > We systematically collected RTL designs from established platforms, including GitHub, Hugging Face, OpenCore, and RISC-V projects, ensuring compliance with open-source licensing requirements.

**Reviewer checklist** for `circuitnet`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

**Evidence** (85 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### cvdp · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][cvdp-s1]
  > a new dataset and infrastructure to advance LLM and agent research in hardware design and verification
- `released` = 2025-06-17 · [S1][cvdp-s1]
  > \[Submitted on 17 Jun 2025\]

#### cvdp · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary engineering-design/circuit-eda; secondary code/code-understanding, agents-tooluse/software-agents · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: Every code generation problem asks for a digital circuit or for the testbench, checker or assertions that verify one, in Verilog or SystemVerilog, and the hidden harness simulates (or for code improvement, synthesises and lints) the result; designing and verifying electronic circuits is circuit-eda's definition, and the paper sets hardware design apart from the software development where LLMs are already used. The family excludes software, which is \`code\`, and \`code\` excludes code that is the means to a result in another field; the boundary is the one VerilogEval's entry logged (taxonomy/\_failures/2026-11-18-verilogeval-001.yaml), which names CVDP, so it is not logged again. The 123 comprehension problems submit an answer about given RTL or testbench code, scored by BLEU or an LLM judge, so no design is submitted; code/code-understanding is secondary and is their subset's primary. The agentic format, an agent working a mini-repository with EDA tools and judged by the harness, makes agents-tooluse/software-agents secondary, as code's exclusion test prescribes for an agentic harness.
  > These categories reflect common subtasks in real-world hardware design and verification workflows.
- `evaluation_method` = execution-tests, reference-metric, model-graded-judge · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: Code generation problems pass or fail by their hidden harness, which simulates the submitted RTL or testbench (Icarus Verilog, Verilator, Yosys, or Cadence Xcelium for categories 12 to 14); correspondence answers (cid06, cid08), expected verbatim, are scored by BLEU against the reference; question-and-answer responses (cid09, cid10) are rated by an LLM judge that compares them with the reference in the context of the question, o4-mini in the paper.
  > A test harness—typically a CocoTB (CocoTB \[2025\]) simulation script—assesses correctness based on task type.
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model, reasoning-model, agent-scaffold · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: The non-agentic format sends one prompt to a model; the paper runs chat models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4.1, Llama 3.1) and reasoning models (o1, o4-mini, Claude 3.7 Sonnet with extended thinking). The agentic format is built for an entrant's Dockerized agent working a mini-repository with tools, which the paper names as the benchmark's purpose, although it ran those problems single-turn (as\_used).
  > Previous benchmarks focus on single-turn prompts and evaluation infrastructure, while CVDP is designed to evaluate agents, with support for tool interaction, iterative workflows, and complex reasoning.
- `secondary_axes` = cost · S5
  - why: LBC-bench rows carry a cost column beside the pass rates.
  > Average cost per test in USD

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `code/function-synthesis` · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: The item is not a self-contained function written from a docstring; each problem is a multi-file repository, and what the harness judges is a simulated circuit or testbench, which VerilogEval's entry kept as its secondary and this entry does not, because most CVDP tasks modify, compose, verify or debug rather than write one unit.
  > represents a multi-file repository extracted at evaluation time.
- `domain` not `code/repository-scale-se` · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: The paper's problems give oracle contexts, only the files needed, so finding where to make the change is not part of the task. v1.1.0's 100 heavy-context problems do work in whole open-source repositories, a minority recorded on their subset.
  > For both Non-Agentic and Agentic problems we limited datapoint creation to oracle contexts
- `domain` not `code/bug-repair` · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: Debugging is one category (47 of 783 problems); the defect is in a circuit and the fix is judged by simulating it, which circuit-eda's verifying covers.
  > cid16 Design Verification - Debugging / Bug Fixing 36 11
- `capability` not `tool-use` · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: The agentic format lets an agent run simulators, but the harness scores the repository the agent leaves, not its tool calls, and the paper ran its agentic problems without tools.
  > Agentic datapoints were converted to Non-Agentic format for evaluation, as no open-source, generalpurpose hardware design agent currently exists.
- `capability` not `optimization` · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: The code improvement category (41 problems) asks for lint fixes or area or latency reductions, but each is passed or failed against stated criteria, not ranked by the objective's value.
  > RTL Lint Improvement or Power -Performance Optimization
- `capability` not `knowledge-recall` · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: The question-answering categories ask about RTL or a testbench given in the prompt, so the answer is read from context; the paper adds that they do not challenge current models.
  > The Question & Answer Code Comprehension datapoints do not sufficiently challenge the LLMs
- `evaluation_method` not `exact-match` · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: Correspondence answers are expected verbatim, but scored by BLEU, a graded overlap, rather than by exact match.
  > should match a reference verbatim
- `designed_for_subjects` not `tool-augmented-model` · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: The non-agentic format offers no tools, and in the agentic format the entrant supplies its own agent image, which is the scaffold.
  > Users populate tool and agent images using provided templates.

#### cvdp · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system Claude 3.7 Sonnet, non-agentic code generation · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  > The highest aggregate pass@1 rate observed was 34% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet)
- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system RTL-Interact-32B, no-commercial non-agentic code generation · [S4][cvdp-s4]
  > On CVDP, RTL-Interact-32B achieves 48.7% weighted Pass@1 and 68.9% Pass@5
- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system Claude Opus 4.8 in Claude Code, heavy-context agentic code generation · S3
  > "name": "Claude Opus 4.8 (Claude Code, xhigh)"
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · S6
  - why: The problems, contexts and harnesses are public and the open-source simulation image builds from the repository. The testbench and assertion categories (and the commercial files) need a Cadence Xcelium licence and a licence network, which a third party can obtain but the benchmark does not supply, and the code generation reference solutions are withheld, so the golden self-check runs only on the repository's example files.
  > NOTE: Requires commercial EDA tools (Cadence Xcelium), license network, and VERIF\_EDA\_IMAGE setup
- `task` = exists true; input non-agentic: one prompt holding the task and its whole context (a specification, RTL, a testbench or a test plan, as the category needs), answered in one turn, agentic: a prompt and a mini-repository in a Docker container, where the entrant's agent can read, edit and run tools such as simulators; output The files the task asks for (RTL modules, testbenches, checkers, assertions, modified, improved or fixed RTL), or for comprehension a code snippet or a text answer.; scoring A hidden harness passes or fails each code generation problem, reported as pass@1 estimated from n = 5 samples; correspondence answers are scored by BLEU against the reference and question-and-answer responses by an LLM judge that compares them with the reference (o4-mini in the paper).; tests_hidden_from_system true; reference_solution true; item_definition A datapoint, a multi-file repository extracted at evaluation time, with its category, difficulty label, prompt, context, harness and reference solution; non-agentic problems are easy or medium, agentic ones span easy to hard. · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  > Models or agents may generate or use a testbench but never see the test harness or reference solution.
- `execution.compute_tier` = simulator-required · S6
  > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = automatable-with-simulator · S6
  - why: A run is automatic end to end, but every code generation verdict comes from simulating the submission in a pinned tool image, whose versions changed in v1.1.0.
  > The build includes cocotb 2.0.1, pytest 8.3.2, Icarus Verilog v13\_0, Yosys yosys-0.40, and Verilator v5.038.
- `execution.harness` = \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\] · S6
  > Run 5 samples for statistical reliability with Pass@1
- `execution.harness_gotcha` · S13
  > Pass@k = 1 - (1 - c/n)^k
- `aggregation_policy` = official-aggregate · [S2][cvdp-s2]

LBC-bench reports each of its three boards as problems passed over problems attempted across the files it includes, with and without the commercial-tool files.

#### cvdp · Data and licence

- `as_used` = protocol Agentic problems run as single-turn prompts. The paper converts every agentic datapoint to the non-agentic format for its Table 3, with the oracle context in the prompt and no tools.; split agentic code generation (166 problems in the paper) · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  > Agentic datapoints were converted to Non-Agentic format for evaluation, as no open-source, generalpurpose hardware design agent currently exists.
- `as_used` = protocol LBC-bench's limited-context board pools the non-agentic and agentic code generation files in one pass rate, and Si2's guidance is to score the agentic files single-turn through the harness's --force-copilot conversion; one row runs Claude Code as the agent.; split code-generation-limited-context (four files, 489 non-agentic and 160 agentic problems in v1.1.0) · S3
  > agentic\_code\_generation\_no\_commercial evaluated non-agentically via --force-copilot per Si2 guidance
- `as_used` = protocol Trained RTL models on the 302 no-commercial non-agentic code generation problems (five categories), allowed to call EDA tools while answering (up to six calls per trajectory, ten for optimisation tasks), scored by pass@1 and pass@5 from five samples at temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95, averaged weighted by category size.; split non-agentic code generation, no-commercial file (302 problems) · [S4][cvdp-s4]
  > temperature 0.7, and top-p 0.95. CVDP averages are weighted by category sizes (94, 78, 55, 40, 35), totaling 302.
- `data.access` = fully-open · S7
  - why: The Hugging Face dataset is ungated and holds every public problem with its context and harness, so anyone can compute the pass rates. The code generation reference solutions are withheld against contamination, which scoring does not need, and 11 of the paper's 783 problems are still unpublished (review\_checks). Running the testbench and assertion categories needs a commercial simulator licence, which gates running them, not reading them.
  > "gated":false
- `data.refresh` = versioned-releases · [S2][cvdp-s2]
  - why: The maintainers release corrected and extended versions with a changelog, and the paper plans further versions as errors are found and as the task set grows.

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `domain`) Family. The submissions are Verilog and SystemVerilog, and CVDP borrows SWE-bench's repository-and-harness design, but what the harness judges is a circuit or a testbench in simulation, and circuit-eda's definition names verifying. This is the HDL boundary VerilogEval's entry logged, which names CVDP; it is not logged again. · [S2][cvdp-s2]
   > By contrast, semiconductor hardware design has not benefited as significantly from LLMs.
2. (field `subsets`) The comprehension subset's override to code/code-understanding rests on its answers being about code rather than designs; by the same boundary a reviewer may keep it in circuit-eda. agents-tooluse/software-agents is secondary for the agentic format although its definition says software engineering.
3. (field `subsets`) Subset modelling. Three formats with their categories as children (19), by 04 S4's scored separately test on Tables 2 to 4, and the v1.1.0 heavy-context set as a fourth subset rather than a variant; the commercial and no-commercial files are not subsets, though LBC-bench reports a pass rate on the no-commercial files alone. A flatter tree of 13 categories is the alternative. · S15
   > Split all datasets into commercial and non-commercial variants
4. (field `versions`) Versions. Six releases are recorded as revisions from the CHANGELOG. v1.0.1 never had files of its own on Hugging Face, and breaking is false for v1.0.2 (a file split) and v1.0.4 (version pinning) by judgement. No public version holds the paper's 783 problems (763 in v1.0.0, 772 from v1.0.2), so the paper's tables cannot be reproduced exactly on public data. · S6
   > Twenty datapoints were omitted from the initial public release release due to test harness issues and licensing restrictions.
5. (field `versions`) v1.1.0's date. Hugging Face added the v1.1.0 files on 2026-05-01 (and LBC-bench's news gives May 1), but Si2's post dates the release to 2026-06-08, when the heavy-context bundles were added; released takes the first. · [S14][cvdp-s14]
   > The latest version called CVDP 1.1.0, released on June 8, 2026, has made the following improvements targeting AI agents
6. (field `governance.independence_flags`) \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\] · S3
   > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
7. (field `governance.submission_process`) \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\] · S5
   > Si2 verification flag
8. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. The harnesses and the comprehension answers are public, some datapoints derive from open-source code, and the heavy-context problems are built on public repositories at recorded commits, so the code they ask for may sit in training corpora; nothing measures it. A reviewer may judge high, at least for the heavy-context subset. · S11
   > See \`manifest.txt\` for original-to-sanitized commit mappings.
9. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) ceiling measured-ceiling rests on the maintainers' own sanity check; with the reference solutions withheld no one else can rerun it, or audit how strict the harnesses are. · [S16][cvdp-s16]
   > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
10. (field `execution.reproducibility_blockers`, needs a specialist) The testbench, checker and assertion categories need a Cadence Xcelium licence; whether that is a licence-restriction blocker beside automatable-with-simulator needs a specialist, as for EngDesign's MATLAB and Cadence tasks. · [S2][cvdp-s2]
   > Some tasks (cid12–14) require commercial tools, currently Cadence Xcelium
11. (field `capability`) capability is empty, by HumanEval's logged gap; verification work (stimulus, checkers, assertions), a third of the problems, may need a term of its own.
12. (field `lineage`) LBC-bench calls itself a benchmark and plans problems beyond CVDP; once an extended set is released it may need its own entry as a fork maintained by Si2. Today its boards run CVDP releases. · S17
   > LBC-bench provides performance data for generation and comprehension of HDLs on design problems by AI models and agents.

**Reviewer checklist** for `cvdp`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

**Evidence** (62 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### engdesign · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][engdesign-s1]
  > In this work, we introduce EngDesign, an Engineering Design benchmark that evaluates LLMs' abilities to perform practical design tasks across nine engineering domains.
- `released` = 2025-07-01 · [S1][engdesign-s1]
  > \[Submitted on 1 Jul 2025 (v1), last revised 6 Nov 2025 (this version, v2)\]
- `release_venue` = NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track · [S1][engdesign-s1]
  > Comments: To Appear in NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks Track

#### engdesign · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary engineering-design/circuit-eda; secondary engineering-design/structural-mechanical-design · [S2][engdesign-s2]
  - why: Every task's scored artifact is a design checked against engineering requirements by simulation, which is the family's inclusion case. Of the paper's nine domains, digital hardware design (17 tasks: Verilog and SystemVerilog modules, HLS kernels, FPGA display logic) and analog IC design (5 SPICE netlists sized for a Spectre testbench) are circuit design, 22 of the 101 tasks and the largest group any engineering-design leaf takes. Structural design (13 tasks: beam, plate, shaft and truss sizing checked in simulation, topology optimisation under load and volume limits) is the secondary, with some of the seven mechanical-systems tasks. Control (18), signal processing (18), robotics (10), operating systems (8) and computer architecture (5) have no leaf in the family. No leaf holds most of the tasks, and the paper's claim is breadth across engineering design, which is ADR-0016's case for an in-family suite leaf; engineering-design has none, so the largest group is primary, as SUPERB's entry did, and the miss is logged. Each domain's leaf, where one exists, is on its subset.
  > spanning practical design problems across nine engineering domains: Operating System Design, Computer Architecture Design, Control System Design, Mechanical Systems, Structural Design, Digital Hardware Design, Analog Integrated Circuit Design, Robotics, and Signal Processing
- `capability` = constraint-satisfaction · [S2][engdesign-s2]
  - why: A task passes only if the design meets every performance requirement the prompt states (margins, settling time, gain, bandwidth, deflection, timing), and the pass rate leads the paper's tables and the board; the paper's contributions name constraint satisfaction. The 0-100 rubric score beside it gives partial credit, which the term does not cover.
  > a binary pass/fail indicator for meeting all performance requirements
- `capability` = reliability-consistency · [S2][engdesign-s2]
  - why: Reasoning robustness, one of the paper's three primary metrics and a column of the board, is the share of tasks passed in all three trials among the tasks passed in any, which scores agreement across repeated runs of the same task.
  > we compute the ratio between the number of tasks where all three trials passed and the number of tasks where at least one trial passed
- `evaluation_method` = execution-tests · [S2][engdesign-s2]
  - why: Each task's script parses the design from the structured response and runs it, through MATLAB toolboxes, SPICE and Cadence Spectre, finite-element and topology-optimisation code, an SSD simulator, Webots or test code, and both the verdict and the rubric points come from whether the simulated behaviour meets the requirements. The term's definition speaks of code; most designs here are parameters, netlists or HDL that a simulator runs, which is logged as a vocabulary miss.
  > These components are then fed into our evaluation pipeline, which runs domain-specific simulations to assess the design
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model, reasoning-model · [S2][engdesign-s2]
  - why: The paper evaluates four chat models and eight reasoning-model configurations, each prompted once per trial through a structured-output schema with no tools and no loop; the board splits the two kinds, and the reasoning effort (o3 and o4-mini at medium or high) and Claude's 16,000-token thinking budget are conditions of the reported numbers.
  > o3 o3-2025-04-16, reasoning effort: medium/high

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `engineering-design/process-control-optimization` · [S2][engdesign-s2]
  - why: The 18 control-design tasks design controllers, but for aircraft, vehicle suspensions, magnetic levitation, a positioning stage and mass-spring systems; one plant, a stirred-tank reactor, is the industrial process the leaf names.
  > Design a stabilizing controller for an aircraft state-space model using MATLAB
- `domain` not `code/function-synthesis` · [S2][engdesign-s2]
  - why: A minority of tasks ask for software, such as the operating-system tasks that implement a block driver and file-system operations and some signal-processing image pipelines, and the paper notes coding implementation tasks. The rest are designs whose simulated performance is scored, which the code family's exclusion leaves to engineering-design.
  > Implement separate programs to perform create, read, update, and delete operations on a provided file system image while maintaining its integrity.
- `domain` not `robotics-embodiment/navigation` · [S2][engdesign-s2]
  - why: The ten robotics tasks compute joint angles, grid paths and trajectories that the evaluator checks or simulates, but no policy acts through a body in an episode; the model submits one answer per trial.
  > Determine the six joint angles of a 6-DOF serial robot that achieve a specified end-effector pose
- `capability` not `optimization` · [S2][engdesign-s2]

Some tasks are calculations or code rather than designs (race-car lap time, a driver's neck load, image statistics, file-system operations); the family is kept because most scored artifacts are designs checked by simulation. · [S2][engdesign-s2]

The stated open split went from 53 to 67 while the commit moved four tasks, and the open folder held 63 tasks before it (GitHub API), so the earlier 53 is unexplained. refresh is versioned-releases on the paper's v2 restating the split; static is arguable, since no task changed. · S4

### 2.7 ISPD Contest (ispd-contest)

`data/benchmarks/engineering-design/ispd-contest.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-18 · last verified 2026-11-18

*The physical-design symposium's yearly contest: a new chip-layout problem each year, scored on hidden testcases.*

The annual contest of the International Symposium on Physical Design (ISPD), held since 2005. Each year an organising team sets one physical-design problem for integrated circuits, releases public testcases and an evaluator, and ranks the submitted tools on testcases held back until the end. The problems have been placement (2005, 2006, 2011, 2014, 2015), global routing (2007, 2008, 2024, 2025), clock-network synthesis (2009, 2010), discrete gate sizing (2012, 2013), FPGA placement (2016, 2017), initial detailed routing (2018, 2019), wafer-scale accelerator placement and physics modelling (2020, 2021), security closure of layouts (2022, 2023) and buffering and sizing (2026, 2027). Entrants submit a tool, not a result: the organisers run it in a fixed environment on the testcases. In ISPD 2026 and 2027 the tool takes a legal placement and netlist in the open ASAP7 library, inserts, removes or resizes buffers, inverters and gates, and must return a legal, logically equivalent design; the OpenROAD-based evaluator routes it and scores post-routing setup timing (TNS, and from 2027 WNS) and power against the unoptimised input, less penalties for hold and electrical-rule violations, runtime, cell displacement and routing overflow. ISPD 2026 had 8 public and 4 hidden testcases and 13 final submissions; ISPD 2027 moves to post-clock-tree designs under multi-corner, multi-mode timing and ranks only on its 8 hidden testcases, with results on 31 March 2027. Past editions' testcases remain standard suites for papers on learned and classical placers and routers.

**Evidence** (48 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### ispd-contest · Identity and id

- `self_description` · S1
  > This contest is built on top of the OpenROAD \[2\] infrastructure and provides a controlled, open-source environment for benchmarking and evaluation.
- `released` = 2005-03-20 · [S2][ispd-contest-s2]
  > 03/20/2005: Six contest benchmarks are posted.
- `release_venue` = ISPD 2005 (International Symposium on Physical Design) · [S3][ispd-contest-s3]
  > ISPD 2005: Placement

#### ispd-contest · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary engineering-design/circuit-eda · S1
  - why: What is scored is a circuit design: in ISPD 2026 and 2027 a placed netlist after buffering and sizing, in earlier editions a placement, a routing solution or a clock network, each judged on timing, power, wirelength, congestion and legality. Placing, routing and sizing electronic circuits is circuit-eda's definition, and the family's inclusion test (a circuit judged against engineering criteria).
  > Contestants must output the modified .v and .def.
- `capability` = optimization · S1
  - why: Every edition states an objective and ranks tools by how well their designs meet it; ISPD 2027 scores normalised improvement over the unoptimised design, setup TNS first, with no known optimum.
  > Setup TNS improvement will remain the primary scoring objective.
- `evaluation_method` = domain-metric, constraint-check · S4
  - why: domain-metric: the evaluator measures the submitted layout with physical-design metrics that have no meaning outside the field, post-routing setup and hold TNS and WNS across corners, dynamic and leakage power, slew, capacitance and fanout violations and routing overflow (HPWL in 2005). constraint-check: placement legality, logical equivalence, clock-tree integrity and the permitted transformations are asserted before scoring, and a design that fails any of them cannot receive a normal score.
  > The evaluator checks a legalized DEF/Verilog pair and measures design quality using global routing and setup/hold timing analysis at BC, TC, and WC.
- `designed_for_subjects` = classical-algorithm, domain-specialist-model · S5
  - why: The entrants are physical-design tools, heuristic and analytical optimisers the teams write: classical-algorithm. ISPD 2024 set out to stimulate GPU- and machine-learning-enhanced global routers, and ISPD 2026 and 2027 invite GPU and ML infrastructure such as PyTorch; a model trained for a routing or sizing step is domain-specialist-model's inclusion test (trained for a task the engineering-design discipline defines), as GANGR's WGAN batching is. Whether any contest entrant was learned is not shown (review\_checks).
  > The goal of this competition is to stimulate academic research aimed at developing a GPU/ML-enhanced global router tailored for industrial-level circuits.

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `constraint-satisfaction` · S1
  - why: Legality, logical equivalence and clock-tree integrity are checked, but a failing design is not simply wrong; its metrics are set just below the worst team's and it is still ranked on them. The score is graded by the objective, not by whether every condition holds.
  > the corresponding metric values are set to 1% worse than the worst value among all teams and baseline for the same design.

#### ispd-contest · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system AlphaRoute (a global router whose rip-up-and-reroute penalties are adjusted by large language models) · [S7][ispd-contest-s7]
  > Crucially, AlphaRoute employs Large Language Models (LLMs) as semantic policy optimizers.
- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system GANGR (net batching for a parallel global router, generated by Wasserstein GANs) · [S9][ispd-contest-s9]

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `versions`) Identity and the counting convention. One family with 23 editions as versions, following CHiME and DCASE: one name, one symposium and a continuing effort. But 04 S4's edition test is "same task definition, new items, new year", and the problem changes most years, so it holds only for runs (2024-2025 global routing, 2026-2027 buffering and sizing). Two alternatives: an entry per edition, since papers cite an edition's testcases on their own for decades (the ISPD 2005 placement suite is still a standard in 2026), which 04 S4's "independently versioned and cited" test for a new benchmark reads on; or an entry per problem line (placement, global routing, detailed routing, clock networks, sizing, security closure). Either needs ids from the lead (04 S3). · [S3][ispd-contest-s3]
   > ISPD 2026: Post-Placement Buffering and Sizing
2. (field `learned_entrant_evidence`) Admissibility (00 S6 A5) rests on two papers that ran learned systems on released testcases after their contests: AlphaRoute (language models tuning a router) on ISPD 2025 and GANGR (WGAN batching) on ISPD 2024. No source read shows a learned system among a contest's own entrants: the registration lists give team names only, ISPD 2026's final leaderboard identifies teams by number, and the 2024 Drive slides and the contest papers were not read. ISPD 2024 set out to stimulate ML-enhanced routers, and ISPD 2026 and 2027 invite ML infrastructure. · S1
   > contestants may (but are not required to) leverage GPU-accelerated solutions or modern ML infrastructure such as PyTorch \[3\]
3. (field `versions`) Seventeen editions (2006 to 2023) are modelled from the Previous Contests page's titles alone; their pages, testcase counts, scoring and winners were not read, nor were the contest papers in the ISPD proceedings or the 2025 description. The ISPD 2021 title, "Wafer-Scale Physics Modeling Contest", may not be a circuit-design problem at all; if not, that edition sits outside circuit-eda. · [S3][ispd-contest-s3]
   > ISPD 2021: Wafer-Scale Physics Modeling Contest
4. (field `activity`) activity accepting-submissions: the 2027 round has opened (registration and public testcases out), but registration closes on 2026-12-05 and the first submission is the alpha on 2027-01-11. round-scheduled is the other reading if the round counts as open only once submissions are taken. · S8
   > Results Announcement: March 31, 2027
5. (field `task.scoring`) The current scoring is not final: the 2027 weights are placeholders until the alpha round, the description says the metric may change, and the flow-runtime limit is still to be set. The task's scoring line and the 2027 version (frozen false) should be re-read after 2027-01-11. · S4
   > Current scores use dummy weights. Final weights will be announced after the Alpha submission.
6. (field `governance.independence_flags`) \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\] · S13
   > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
7. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method domain-metric with constraint-check. composite is rejected because the sub-scores all come from one evaluation flow (timing, power, ERC, overflow and displacement, plus the flow's runtime); a reviewer who counts runtime as a different method would add composite. entrant-relative-ranking is rejected though a failing design is valued at 1% worse than the worst team. · S1
   > All design-quality metrics are normalized against the corresponding metrics of the baseline.
8. (field `data.access`) data.access fully-open is a finished edition's state (ISPD 2026's hidden testcases are on its page); ISPD 2027 is private-test-server until it concludes. ISPD 2026 also ranked on its public testcases, which its organisers called a weakness after a withdrawn submission. · S13
   > we will use more rigorous evaluations (e.g., only on hidden testcases)
9. (field `execution.reproducibility_tier`) reproducibility\_tier automatable-with-simulator with specific-simulator-build, and data\_provenance simulation-generated, both treat the OpenROAD flow (routing, extraction, static timing) as the simulator, as circuitnet treats its EDA tools. If an EDA flow is not a simulator in these terms' sense, the tier is fully-automatable and the provenance needs a term for tool-generated design data.
10. (field `designed_for_subjects`) designed\_for\_subjects domain-specialist-model rests on the ISPD 2024 contest's stated aim and on ML being invited in 2026 and 2027; classical-algorithm alone is the reading if the contest is taken as designed for heuristic tools, which the winners' team names and the 2026 rules (rank only teams that implement their own methods) neither confirm nor rule out. · S5
   > The goal of this competition is to stimulate academic research aimed at developing a GPU/ML-enhanced global router tailored for industrial-level circuits.

### 2.8 EngiBench (ideallab-engibench)

`data/benchmarks/engineering-design/ideallab-engibench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-18 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Simulator-backed engineering design problems, from beam topology to airfoils and photonics, for generative models.*

An open-source Python library and set of datasets for data-driven engineering design from the IDEAL Lab at ETH Zurich, whose problem implementations were developed at the University of Maryland. Each problem pairs a simulator with a Hugging Face dataset of optimised designs and the conditions they were optimised for, behind one API: the design space, objectives and conditions, a constraint check, simulate, and for most problems an adjoint optimiser that polishes a design. The paper's release (v0.0.1, May 2025) has seven problems: Airfoil (shape optimisation with RANS in MachAero, matching a lift coefficient at least drag), HeatConduction2D and 3D (placing conductive material for least thermal compliance), ThermoElastic2D (structural and thermal compliance), Beams2D (an MBB beam's compliance, after the 88-line topology optimisation code), Photonics2D (a wavelength demultiplexer in the ceviche FDFD solver) and PowerElectronics (sizing a DC-DC converter simulated in NgSpice). Thermoelastic3D followed in v0.2.0 (March 2026), and Beams3D and MTO2D (thermofluid topology optimisation in OpenFOAM) are on the unreleased main branch, ten problems in all. The paper scores generated designs per problem on five measures: MMD to the dataset's designs, DPP diversity, the cumulative optimality gap (COG) of a generated design refined by the problem's optimiser against the best known objective, the ratio of designs violating a constraint (RVC) and the ratio of failed simulations (RF). Its baselines, from the companion library EngiOpt, are GANs and diffusion models for inverse design and MLP surrogates with NSGA-II, ten seeds each, with 50 test conditions sampled per run; the authors present them as a proof of concept, not a comprehensive benchmark. No aggregate is defined. EngiOpt has since added a leaderboard that re-scores each checkpoint before ranking it within one problem and evaluation spec, but only the lab can submit, and the board could not be read. Problems are versioned on their own: Photonics2D v1 (2026) fixes a v0 bug by which re-simulated designs did not reproduce their stored objectives.

#### ideallab-engibench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary engineering-design/structural-mechanical-design; secondary engineering-design/circuit-eda, physics/optics-photonics · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
  - why: Every problem's scored artifact is a design (a material layout, an airfoil shape, a photonic device, a set of circuit parameters) that the problem's simulator evaluates against engineering objectives and constraints, which is the family's inclusion test. No engineering-design leaf takes most problems and the paper's claim is breadth across domains. The structural problems are the largest group a leaf names: Beams2D and ThermoElastic2D of the paper's seven, with Beams3D and Thermoelastic3D added, four of ten. PowerElectronics sizes a converter circuit (circuit-eda) and Photonics2D designs an optical demultiplexer (optics-photonics: "designing optical and photonic systems"). The two heat-conduction problems, Airfoil and MTO2D have no leaf (logged as taxonomy/\_failures/2026-11-18-ideallab-engibench-001).
  > as well as in physics domain, including aerodynamics, structural elasticity, thermal diffusion, and power electronics
- `capability` = optimization · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
  - why: Each problem states objectives (compliance, drag at a target lift, field overlap, DC gain error and voltage ripple), and COG scores how far a generated design, refined by the problem's optimiser, stays from the best known objective; the 2026 flow-matching paper takes COG and a final gap as its primary metrics.
  > The cumulative optimality gap (COG) measures how far a generated design lags behind the best known objective value throughout the optimization process.
- `capability` = constraint-satisfaction · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
  - why: RVC counts a generated design as failing if any of the problem's inequality or equality constraints is violated, and every problem has a constraint check; the paper claims feasibility under hard constraints as a contribution.
  > The ratio of violated constraints (RVC) measures how many generated samples fail to satisfy constraints on the designs.
- `capability` = generation-fidelity · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
  - why: For inverse-design models MMD compares the generated designs with the dataset's optimised designs for the sampled conditions, which is closeness to a reference distribution.
  > A common metric is maximum mean discrepancy (MMD, \[23\]), which measures the distance between two distributions.
- `evaluation_method` = domain-metric, statistical-fit, constraint-check · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
  - why: domain-metric for COG and the objectives behind it, computed by each problem's simulator in its own engineering units (compliance, drag coefficient, field overlap, DC gain), with the best known objective estimated by the problem's adjoint optimiser; statistical-fit for MMD, a two-sample distance between the generated and the dataset's designs, as guacamol records its KL benchmark; constraint-check for RVC, the problem's constraint check applied to each design before simulation. RF counts designs whose simulation failed. The score comes from running the problem's simulator on each submitted design, which no term names (logged as taxonomy/\_failures/2026-11-18-ideallab-engibench-002).
  > typically estimated using an adjoint solver
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model, classical-algorithm · [S1][ideallab-engibench-s1]
  - why: The intended entrants are inverse-design and surrogate models trained from scratch on each problem's dataset (GANs, diffusion models, MLP surrogates), for a task the engineering-design discipline defines: domain-specialist-model's inclusion test. The library is also stated to compare optimisation algorithms, which contain no learned component; but the paper and the EngiOpt board score only learned models, and the problems' own optimisers serve as the reference that produces the datasets and the best known objective (review\_checks).
  > EngiBench provides a unified API and a curated set of benchmarks -- covering aeronautics, heat conduction, photonics, and more -- that enable fair, reproducible comparisons of optimization and machine learning algorithms, such as generative or surrogate models.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `physics/simulation-surrogates` · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
  - why: Surrogate-based optimisation is one supported paradigm, and the paper's PowerElectronics experiment compares its surrogates' Pareto fronts with NgSpice's. But that is one experiment of four, the cross-domain study and the EngiOpt board score generated designs, and the problems' simulators score the designs rather than standing as the reference a learned emulator is fitted to (review\_checks).
  > confirmed that the surrogate and NgSpicegenerated fronts stem from different distributions
- `capability` not `creativity-novelty` · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
  - why: DPP rewards spread-out designs but measures variety with no usefulness criterion, which the term's exclusion rules out. EngiOpt's board measures novelty and a copy rate, keeps them unranked and leaves memorising rows out of the ranking, which is close to penalising reproduction (review\_checks).
  > Determinantal point processes (DPP, \[37\]) quantify diversity by favoring well-spread-out samples.
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
  - why: The heat-conduction test split holds out two volume and two adiabatic-region values from training, a deliberate shift, but in one problem pair only and with no separately reported out-of-distribution score.
  > we randomly excluded two unique values of the volume limit and two unique values of the adiabatic region from the training set

- `execution.harness` = EngiBench's problem classes (check\_constraints, simulate, optimize) with EngiOpt's shared evaluator (python -m engiopt.evaluate) and its frozen evaluation specs · [S9][ideallab-engibench-s9]
  > The committed evaluation specs are frozen against the current EngiBench, whose \`photonics2d\` and \`thermoelastic2d\` read the \`v1\` datasets; the newest PyPI release (0.2.0) still points those two at \`v0\`.
- `aggregation_policy` = none-by-design · [S9][ideallab-engibench-s9]

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `id`) Identity. Two unrelated benchmarks are called EngiBench, so under the allocation rules' shared-name rule ("the id carries a disambiguator (the maintainer or the game)") this one is ideallab-engibench, after the maintainer's GitHub organisation, as futuresearch-deep-research-bench carries its maintainer first. engibench-ideallab, or the bare engibench with the other taking a disambiguator, are the other readings. The other EngiBench (arXiv 2509.17677) was not drafted. Id allocation is a human act (04 S3). · [S1][ideallab-engibench-s1]
   > we introduce EngiBench, the first open-source library and datasets spanning diverse domains for data-driven engineering design
2. (field `versions`) Versions. The library's releases are versions (0.0.1 and 0.1.0 revisions, 0.2.0 a track-set that adds Thermoelastic3D), and the unreleased main branch is an unfrozen version because EngiOpt's specs are frozen against it. Problems are also versioned on their own (Beams2D v1, Photonics2D v1, several v1 and v2 datasets), recorded in the subsets' notes and the errata. A reviewer may prefer per-problem versions, since a score is defined by problem version, dataset version and spec version, not by library release.
3. (field `versions`) Photonics2D v0, used in the paper's cross-domain study, did not reproduce stored objectives on re-simulation (up to about 37 times off). The paper's Photonics2D numbers and any later v0 result are not comparable with v1, and the paper's other problems may need the same check. · [S15][ideallab-engibench-s15]
   > so an optimized design did not reproduce its reported objective when re-simulated
4. (field `lineage`) EngiOpt is counted as the harness and baselines of this entry, and its leaderboard as this benchmark's board: same organisation, and its specs and rows are per EngiBench problem. Its board has its own spec versions, metrics (iog, fog, viol beside mmd and dpp) and ranking flags, so under 04 S4 it could be a separate benchmark linked by lineage. EngiAI (arXiv 2605.19743) is filed as a use; it is a framework with its own tiers and scores built on two problems and could be its own entry.
5. (field `activity`) The EngiOpt leaderboard (Hugging Face IDEALLab/engiopt-leaderboard) answered HTTP 401, so no row, date or entrant was read, and only accounts with write access can submit. activity no-submission-channel and submission\_process maintainer-run rest on that; leaderboard-live-no-round, or literature-only if the board is not yet live, are the other readings. · [S7][ideallab-engibench-s7]
   > The last step needs write access to the board repository.
6. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark is set because only the maintainer's organisation can put rows on the board, and the board ranks EngiOpt's models. The paper's baselines are the maintainers' too. Both 2026 papers read here extend EngiOpt; their affiliations were not read, so whether any use is independent of the maintainers is open, and is a reviewer's call.
7. (field `domain`) Domain. structural-mechanical-design is primary as the largest group a leaf names (two of the paper's seven problems, four of ten now), not a majority: the heat-conduction problems, Airfoil and MTO2D have no leaf (taxonomy/\_failures/2026-11-18-ideallab-engibench-001). physics/simulation-surrogates is rejected, though surrogate modelling is a supported paradigm and the paper's PowerElectronics experiment scores surrogate Pareto fronts against NgSpice.
8. (field `data.dataset_licence`) Dataset licence. The README and the paper say CC-BY-NC-SA for all datasets, but the Hugging Face records tag mto\_2d\_v0 as MIT and give photonics\_2d\_120\_120\_v1 no licence tag, and the newer v1 and v2 records were not all read. · [S13][ideallab-engibench-s13]
   > "tags":\["license:mit"
9. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium: the scored test conditions come with their optimised designs in public splits, and the maintainers write that a lookup table posts a perfect MMD; the board's copy rate keeps such a row out of the ranking, and a spec scoring conditions with no published design is proposed, not built. high is the other reading if releasing the reference designs beside the scored conditions counts as a protocol that evaluates on the data it releases. · [S7][ideallab-engibench-s7]
   > A v2 spec would draw conditions from the condition space rather than from dataset rows
10. (field `release_venue`) release\_venue rests on the README's citation (NeurIPS 2025 proceedings, an OpenReview forum). The track (main or Datasets and Benchmarks) and the decision were not read: OpenReview's API returned a challenge page (403), and the arXiv v2 is preprint-styled. · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
   > Learning and optimization library code: https://github.com/IDEALLab/EngiOpt. Preprint.
11. (field `designed_for_subjects`) classical-algorithm is tagged from the stated aim (comparing optimisation and machine-learning algorithms), but no non-learned entrant is scored in the sources read; the problems' own optimisers produce the datasets and the best known objective. Drop it if only learned entrants are intended; evaluation\_target would then be learned-system.
12. (field `evaluation_method`) Metrics drift. The paper defines COG, MMD, DPP, RVC and RF; EngiOpt's board and the 2026 flow-matching paper use a final optimality gap (fog) and an initial one (iog) and call constraint violation viol, which were not read in their definitions. A score labelled COG and one labelled fog are not the same measure. The paper also warns its own baseline results should not be overinterpreted. · [S4][ideallab-engibench-s4]
   > These results are surprising and should not be overinterpreted

**Reviewer checklist** for `ideallab-engibench`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

### 2.10 Learn2Design (learn2design-2026)

`data/benchmarks/engineering-design/learn2design-2026.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-18 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Optimisers submitted as code tune about 200 parameters of hidden gravitational-wave detector designs in a simulator.*

A NeurIPS 2026 competition from the Artificial Scientist Lab at the University of Tübingen on the automated design of gravitational-wave detectors. Each task is a detector topology drawn from the quasi-universal interferometer (UIFO), a grid of beam splitters, lasers, squeezers and one detector, with roughly 200 continuous parameters such as laser powers, mirror reflectivities and distances. Entrants submit an optimisation algorithm, not a design: a Python class that receives dfbench's Objective, which wraps the differentiable JAX simulator Differometor and logs every evaluation. The organisers ran each submission for up to four hours per topology on one H100 GPU. A run scores the lowest loss among the setups that satisfy the physical power constraints, where the loss compares the design's broadband strain sensitivity with the Voyager reference detector on a log scale (zero is reference level, negative is better); the score is the mean over ten hidden topologies. Three monthly public rounds and a final round (Round 4, 110 participants) ran from August to October 2026, beside seven organiser baselines from random search to CMA-ES and Adam. A corpus of 29,650 optimised designs is released for training surrogates, warm starts or generative models. Prizes of EUR 25,000 are sponsored by SPRIND, and the winners are announced at NeurIPS on 2026-12-11.

#### learn2design-2026 · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary engineering-design/experimental-apparatus-design; secondary physics/optics-photonics · S1
  - why: What is scored is a design of a physical instrument, an interferometric gravitational-wave detector, found by the submitted algorithm and judged by its simulated sensitivity under physical constraints: the family's inclusion test (an apparatus judged against engineering criteria), and the family's own example. The detector is an optical system of mirrors, beam splitters, lasers and squeezed-light sources, which is physics/optics-photonics ("designing optical and photonic systems").
  > An interferometric detector can be represented as a graph-like optical experiment
- `capability` = optimization · S2
  - why: The benchmark states an objective, the simulator's loss, and ranks systems by the mean of the best feasible values they reach, which is the term's inclusion test; the difficulty is the best design, not any feasible one.
  > The arithmetic mean over the 10 recorded losses is your score. Lower is better.
- `capability` = experimental-design · S1
  - why: The scored artifact is an apparatus, a detector design, and the taxonomy names this benchmark as the term's example. It is judged by its sensitivity, a property of the instrument, rather than by whether it would discriminate between hypotheses (review\_checks).
  > Can machine learning algorithms discover experimental designs that go beyond human intuition, while remaining physically meaningful and experimentally constrained?
- `capability` = search-exploration · S4
  - why: Each run is a search over about 200 continuous parameters under a four-hour wall-clock budget, and only what was found inside the budget counts, which is discovery under a budget; the first tie-breaker is the time taken to reach the best loss.
  > loss reached within the 4-hour wall-clock budget
- `evaluation_method` = domain-metric · S5
  - why: The loss is defined within gravitational-wave detector design: the candidate's broadband strain-sensitivity curve against the Voyager reference detector on a log scale, plus penalties from the optical power constraints. It is the competition's own measure rather than one standardised across the field (review\_checks).
  > compares the candidate detector's broadband strain-sensitivity curve to the Voyager reference detector on a log scale
- `designed_for_subjects` = classical-algorithm, domain-specialist-model · S1
  - why: The seven organiser baselines are non-learned optimisers (Adam variants, SGD with momentum, BFGS, L-BFGS, CMA-ES, random search), and the proposal sets such optimisers against amortised learned methods. Those are trained for this engineering-design task on the released design corpus, which the rules encourage for pre-training surrogates and warm starts, with pretrained weights shipped in the submission: domain-specialist-model's inclusion test (trained from scratch for a task the discipline defines).
  > allowing classical optimizers such as Adam, BFGS, and Bayesian optimization to compete directly with amortized methods such as prior-fitted networks

**Open review checks** (11):

1. Identity. The id is learn2design-2026, the name the taxonomy's three examples use (domains.yaml, the engineering-design family; capabilities.yaml, experimental-design and hypothesis-generation), as calochallenge-2022 and lhc-olympics-2020 name dated one-off competitions. The other reading is \`learn2design\` with 2026 as its first edition (04 S4: a re-issue on the same task is a version), which would move those refs; it fits only if a recurring series is announced. Id allocation is a human act (04 S3). The proposal calls it a new competition, not a recurring series, and no 2027 edition is announced. · S1
   > Learn2Design is an entirely new competition and is not a continuation of any previously accepted NeurIPS competition or recurring benchmark series.
2. (field `learned_entrant_evidence`) Admissibility (00 S6 A5). No learned entrant's score is published: the README's seven baselines are all non-learned, VAESampling is a dfbench algorithm with no UIFO result found, and the VAE warm start is a planned baseline. The entrants' methods are confidential until the joint review paper. Re-read after 2026-12-11.
3. (field `data.access`) Round 4 is read as the final evaluation: it scored the submissions due on the final deadline, the commit calls its ten-UIFO results official, and the top ten were run on forty more topologies, as the proposal planned for the final. The scoring rules say the final topologies are never published, yet Round 4's seeds are. If the final ranking is a separate private evaluation, access is private-test-server and the tier not-independently-reproducible with private-test-set. · S4
   > hidden topologies, which are never published
4. (field `activity`) activity results-pending: the ranking is published (2026-10-27) but the official winners come after the source-code review, on 2026-12-11. closed is the other reading now, and after that date. The site still says "Submissions open"; the Codabench portal did not connect on 2026-11-17 and was not retried. · [S10][learn2design-2026-s10]
   > Portal status Submissions open
5. (field `capability`) hypothesis-generation is rejected against the taxonomy's own example, because only the best design of each run is scored. experimental-design is kept as the taxonomy's example has it, though the design is judged by sensitivity, not by discriminating between hypotheses.
6. (field `evaluation_method`) domain-metric for a loss the simulator defines; it is the competition's own, not a measure standardised across gravitational-wave instrumentation, and no term names a score computed by re-running a simulator on the submission (logged as taxonomy/\_failures/2026-11-18-learn2design-2026-001, the second case of the open simulator-reevaluation proposal).
7. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark is not set although the seven organiser baselines are plotted beside the 110 entrants; the rules bar organisers from competing. arc-agi-3 set the flag for reference harnesses on its own board. · S2
   > compares all \*\*110 participants on the same ten UIFOs\*\*, alongside the seven organizer baselines
8. (field `lineage`) Differometor-Benchmark (dfbench) is counted as the harness. It is versioned on its own (v0.2.0 to v0.3.3, last pushed 2026-11-12) and has its own problems (Voyager, ConstrainedVoyager) and benchmark runner, so under 04 S4 it could be a separate entry linked by lineage. · S7
   > A benchmarking framework for optimization algorithms on gravitational-wave detector design problems
9. (field `domain`) physics/optics-photonics as secondary rests on the detector being an optical system; the physics family's inclusion test (a simulated physical process scored) also fits, so a reviewer may prefer it primary. The family's own example puts the benchmark in engineering-design.
10. (field `data.refresh`) refresh periodic-recompetition rests on the rounds of one edition each using new topologies; static is the reading if no edition follows 2026.
11. (field `comparability`) The hardware moved from the proposal's A100 to an H100 evaluation VM. The budget is wall-clock time, so results from other hardware, or from the proposal's specification, are not on the same footing (hardware\_platform is material). · S2
   > Its original hardware specifications are superseded by the \[current evaluation specification\]

**Reviewer checklist** for `learn2design-2026`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist
